claim: In the CCK-DsRed mouse strain, 84% of DsRed-expressing interneurons showed immunopositivity for CCK.
source: In the CCK-DsRed mouse strain, 84% of DsRed-expressing interneurons showed immunopositivity for CCK, and 92% of CCK-immunoreactive cells had DsRed expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Data obtained from immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: In the CCK-DsRed mouse strain, 92% of CCK-immunoreactive cells had DsRed expression.
source: In the CCK-DsRed mouse strain, 84% of DsRed-expressing interneurons showed immunopositivity for CCK, and 92% of CCK-immunoreactive cells had DsRed expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Data obtained from immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: In the PV-eGFP mouse strain, 95% of eGFP-expressing interneurons had immunolabeling for PV.
source: In the PV-eGFP mouse strain, 95% of eGFP-expressing interneurons had immunolabeling for PV, and 92% of PV-immunostained neurons showed eGFP expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Data obtained from immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: In the PV-eGFP mouse strain, 92% of PV-immunostained neurons showed eGFP expression.
source: In the PV-eGFP mouse strain, 95% of eGFP-expressing interneurons had immunolabeling for PV, and 92% of PV-immunostained neurons showed eGFP expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Data obtained from immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Only 2–3% of cells in PV-eGFPxCCK-DsRed double transgenic mice expressed both fluorescent proteins.
source: Quantification of the overlap between eGFP and DsRed expression in PV-eGFPxCCK-DsRed double transgenic mice (n = 2 mice) showed that only 2–3% of the cells expressed both fluorescent proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Data obtained from quantification in double transgenic mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Double labeled neurons expressing both eGFP and DsRed had small soma size, dense local dendritic and axonal arborization, and a firing character of late-spiking phenotype, features that typify neurogliaform cells.
source: These double labeled neurons had small soma size, dense local dendritic and axonal arborization as well as a firing character of late-spiking phenotype, features that together typify neurogliaform cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) (Mańko et al., 2012).
evidence: Morphological and electrophysiological characterization combined with citation to previous work on neurogliaform cells

claim: The vast majority of intracellularly labeled DsRed-expressing interneurons showed CB1 immunoreactivity (97%, n = 30).
source: The vast majority of the intracellularly labeled DsRed-expressing interneurons showed CB1 immunoreactivity (97%, n = 30, Figure 1B), and all the tested PVBCs expressed a calcium binding protein calbindin (100%, n = 7, Figure 1D), as we reported previously (Vereczki et al., 2016).
evidence: Data from immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 1B with reference to previous publication

claim: All tested PVBCs expressed the calcium binding protein calbindin (100%, n = 7).
source: The vast majority of the intracellularly labeled DsRed-expressing interneurons showed CB1 immunoreactivity (97%, n = 30, Figure 1B), and all the tested PVBCs expressed a calcium binding protein calbindin (100%, n = 7, Figure 1D), as we reported previously (Vereczki et al., 2016).
evidence: Data from immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 1D with reference to previous publication

claim: PVBCs showed the characteristic fast spiking phenotype.
source: When tested with square current pulses, PVBCs showed the characteristic fast spiking phenotype, while CCKBCs displayed a slower, regular firing pattern in accordance with previous data (Jasnow et al., 2009; Rainnie et al., 2006; Woodruff and Sah, 2007) (Figure 1E,G).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1G with citations to previous studies

claim: CCKBCs displayed a slower, regular firing pattern.
source: When tested with square current pulses, PVBCs showed the characteristic fast spiking phenotype, while CCKBCs displayed a slower, regular firing pattern in accordance with previous data (Jasnow et al., 2009; Rainnie et al., 2006; Woodruff and Sah, 2007) (Figure 1E,G).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1E with citations to previous studies

claim: The probability to find a synaptically connected neighboring (<~150 µm) PN was 85% for CCKBCs.
source: The probability to find a synaptically connected neighboring (<~150 µm) PN was high in both cases (85% for CCKBCs and 81% for PVBCs, respectively, n = 40 CCKBC and n = 37 PVBC).
evidence: Data from paired recording experiments

claim: The probability to find a synaptically connected neighboring (<~150 µm) PN was 81% for PVBCs.
source: The probability to find a synaptically connected neighboring (<~150 µm) PN was high in both cases (85% for CCKBCs and 81% for PVBCs, respectively, n = 40 CCKBC and n = 37 PVBC).
evidence: Data from paired recording experiments

claim: The estimated reversal potentials of the PSPs recorded in perforated patch and whole-cell mode showed no significant difference.
source: The estimated reversal potentials of the PSPs recorded in perforated patch and whole-cell mode showed no significant difference (Figure 1K), therefore, in further experiments, we used the 4 mM Cl− containing intrapipette solution.
evidence: Statistical comparison of reversal potentials measured in two recording modes shown in Figure 1K

claim: The reversal potential of the PSPs arriving from both interneuron types were at more hyperpolarized values than the resting membrane potential of the PN.
source: Furthermore, we found that the reversal potential of the PSPs arriving from both interneuron types were at more hyperpolarized values than the resting membrane potential of the PN, implying that the net effect of these BCs on their postsynaptic PN partners is inhibitory (p<0.001, Wilcoxon Signed Rank test, Figure 1K).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 1K with p-value

claim: The net effect of CCKBCs and PVBCs on their postsynaptic PN partners is inhibitory.
source: Furthermore, we found that the reversal potential of the PSPs arriving from both interneuron types were at more hyperpolarized values than the resting membrane potential of the PN, implying that the net effect of these BCs on their postsynaptic PN partners is inhibitory (p<0.001, Wilcoxon Signed Rank test, Figure 1K).
evidence: Inference from reversal potential measurements with statistical support

claim: IPSCs originating from PVBCs had significantly shorter latencies than those from CCKBCs.
source: Importantly, the latency of the signals indicated the monosynaptic nature of the connections from both cell types, however, IPSCs originating from PVBCs had significantly shorter latencies than those from CCKBCs.
evidence: Comparison of latency measurements from paired recordings

claim: The failure rate, potency and amplitude of the first IPSC were not significantly different between CCKBCs and PVBCs.
source: The failure rate, potency and amplitude of the first IPSC were not significantly different.
evidence: Statistical comparison of IPSC properties

claim: Events arriving from PVBCs had faster rise time but similar decay time compared to CCKBCs.
source: The events arriving from PVBCs had faster rise time but similar decay time.
evidence: Comparison of IPSC kinetics from paired recordings

claim: IPSCs originating from PVBCs onto PNs showed uniformly a marked depression.
source: In addition, there was a significant difference in the short-term plasticity of the signals: IPSCs originating from PVBCs onto PNs showed uniformly a marked depression, while those arising from CCKBCs were more variable and showed only a slight depression on average.
evidence: Analysis of short-term plasticity from paired recordings

claim: IPSCs arising from CCKBCs were more variable and showed only a slight depression on average.
source: In addition, there was a significant difference in the short-term plasticity of the signals: IPSCs originating from PVBCs onto PNs showed uniformly a marked depression, while those arising from CCKBCs were more variable and showed only a slight depression on average.
evidence: Analysis of short-term plasticity from paired recordings

claim: The charge transfer of the IPSCs and the area of IPSPs evoked by CCKBCs and PVBCs in response to three action potentials at 30 Hz were not significantly different.
source: Importantly, the charge transfer of the IPSCs and the area of IPSPs evoked by the two BCs in response to three action potentials at 30 Hz were not significantly different.
evidence: Statistical comparison of IPSC and IPSP properties

claim: Both CCKBCs and PVBCs could silence their postsynaptic partners with ~75% probability on average.
source: When we compared the inhibitory efficacy of CCKBCs and PVBCs (i.e. 1- the probability of PN spiking in the presence of BC firing) we could not find significant differences. Both BC types could silence their postsynaptic partners with ~75% probability on average (Figure 2C).
evidence: Data from spike inhibition experiments shown in Figure 2C

claim: 42% of CCKBCs could veto PN firing with very high probability (>95% inhibitory efficacy).
source: However, in both cell types there were BCs, which could veto PN firing with very high probability (>95% inhibitory efficacy, 42% of CCKBCs and 45% of PVBCs, n = 8 and 9, respectively), whereas others had only a weak inhibitory efficacy (<50% inhibitory efficacy, 21% of CCKBCs and 20% of PVBCs, n = 4 and 4, respectively).
evidence: Quantification of inhibitory efficacy across BC populations

claim: 45% of PVBCs could veto PN firing with very high probability (>95% inhibitory efficacy).
source: However, in both cell types there were BCs, which could veto PN firing with very high probability (>95% inhibitory efficacy, 42% of CCKBCs and 45% of PVBCs, n = 8 and 9, respectively), whereas others had only a weak inhibitory efficacy (<50% inhibitory efficacy, 21% of CCKBCs and 20% of PVBCs, n = 4 and 4, respectively).
evidence: Quantification of inhibitory efficacy across BC populations

claim: 21% of CCKBCs had only a weak inhibitory efficacy (<50% inhibitory efficacy).
source: However, in both cell types there were BCs, which could veto PN firing with very high probability (>95% inhibitory efficacy, 42% of CCKBCs and 45% of PVBCs, n = 8 and 9, respectively), whereas others had only a weak inhibitory efficacy (<50% inhibitory efficacy, 21% of CCKBCs and 20% of PVBCs, n = 4 and 4, respectively).
evidence: Quantification of inhibitory efficacy across BC populations

claim: 20% of PVBCs had only a weak inhibitory efficacy (<50% inhibitory efficacy).
source: However, in both cell types there were BCs, which could veto PN firing with very high probability (>95% inhibitory efficacy, 42% of CCKBCs and 45% of PVBCs, n = 8 and 9, respectively), whereas others had only a weak inhibitory efficacy (<50% inhibitory efficacy, 21% of CCKBCs and 20% of PVBCs, n = 4 and 4, respectively).
evidence: Quantification of inhibitory efficacy across BC populations

claim: BCs that gave rise to IPSPs with larger area had a more pronounced inhibitory effect on their postsynaptic partner's spiking.
source: Those BCs that gave rise to IPSPs with larger area had a more pronounced inhibitory effect on their postsynaptic partner's spiking (Figure 2D).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: The IPSP area correlated well with the charge transfer of IPSCs.
source: Therefore, we used the charge transfer of IPSCs as the key electrophysiological property at a BC-PN connection, which correlated well with the IPSP area (Figure 2E) and similarly related to the inhibitory efficacy of BCs (Figure 2F).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: IPSPs which failed to veto PN firing could still alter the timing of the spike, delaying it by up to 38.5 ms.
source: We observed that IPSPs which failed to veto PN firing, could still alter the timing of the spike, delaying it by up to 38.5 ms (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: Data from spike timing experiments shown in Figure 2G-I

claim: The maximal delay caused by CCKBCs and PVBCs was not significantly different.
source: The maximal delay caused by the two BC types was not significantly different (Figure 2I).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 2I

claim: Both CCKBCs and PVBCs could control the firing of PNs in a ~110 ms-long time window.
source: We found that both cell types could control the firing of PNs in a ~110 ms-long time window (Figure 2I), with increased delaying effect in PN firing as the IPSP arrived closer to the sinusoidal cycle peak (i.e. to the theoretical time of the spike).
evidence: Data from timing experiments shown in Figure 2I

claim: 85.4% of the potential contact sites (based on confocal microscopic analysis) formed synaptic junctions on the soma or dendrites of the postsynaptic PNs.
source: Correlated light and electron microscopic investigations showed that 85.4% of the potential contact sites (based on the confocal microscopic analysis) formed synaptic junctions on the soma (87.5%, n = 16 terminals from six pairs, Figure 3E and G) or dendrites (83.3%, n = 18 terminals from six pairs, Figure 3F and G) of the postsynaptic PNs (see detailed description of the analyzed contact numbers in Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Correlated light and electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3E-G

claim: 87.5% of potential contact sites on the soma formed synaptic junctions (n = 16 terminals from six pairs).
source: Correlated light and electron microscopic investigations showed that 85.4% of the potential contact sites (based on the confocal microscopic analysis) formed synaptic junctions on the soma (87.5%, n = 16 terminals from six pairs, Figure 3E and G) or dendrites (83.3%, n = 18 terminals from six pairs, Figure 3F and G) of the postsynaptic PNs (see detailed description of the analyzed contact numbers in Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3E and G

claim: 83.3% of potential contact sites on dendrites formed synaptic junctions (n = 18 terminals from six pairs).
source: Correlated light and electron microscopic investigations showed that 85.4% of the potential contact sites (based on the confocal microscopic analysis) formed synaptic junctions on the soma (87.5%, n = 16 terminals from six pairs, Figure 3E and G) or dendrites (83.3%, n = 18 terminals from six pairs, Figure 3F and G) of the postsynaptic PNs (see detailed description of the analyzed contact numbers in Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3F and G

claim: Both CCKBCs and PVBCs established synapses on thick (>1 µm) and thin (<0.5 µm) dendritic segments at the same ratio.
source: In addition, we found that the diameter of the targeted dendrites was variable, i.e. both cell types established synapses on thick (>1 µm, CCKBCs n = 10, PVBCs n = 6), presumably proximal and thin (<0.5 µm, CCKBCs n = 12, PVBCs n = 10), presumably distal dendritic segments at the same ratio (Figure 3H).
evidence: Electron microscopy analysis of dendrite diameters shown in Figure 3H

claim: The comparison of the target distribution of CCKBCs and PVBCs along the PN membrane surface revealed no difference.
source: The comparison of the target distribution of the two BC types along the PN membrane surface revealed no difference (Figure 4C–E), i.e. they targeted the same somato-dendritic compartment of PNs (Figure 4E,K–S test p=0.29), covering the whole length of the dendritic tree with exponentially decreasing density of contacts towards the tip of the dendrites (Figure 4F).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 4C-E with K-S test p-value

claim: CCKBCs and PVBCs covered the whole length of the dendritic tree with exponentially decreasing density of contacts towards the tip of the dendrites.
source: The comparison of the target distribution of the two BC types along the PN membrane surface revealed no difference (Figure 4C–E), i.e. they targeted the same somato-dendritic compartment of PNs (Figure 4E,K–S test p=0.29), covering the whole length of the dendritic tree with exponentially decreasing density of contacts towards the tip of the dendrites (Figure 4F).
evidence: Analysis of contact distribution shown in Figure 4F

claim: CCKBCs and PVBCs innervated their postsynaptic partners with similar number of boutons.
source: We found that CCKBCs and PVBCs innervated their postsynaptic partners with similar number of boutons (Figure 4G), moreover, the average distance of the innervation along the dendritic tree (Figure 4H), the number of the contacts established on the perisomatic region (Figure 4I) and the ratio of perisomatic contacts among all boutons showed no significant difference (Figure 4J, all M-W test, p>0.05).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 4G with M-W test

claim: The average distance of the innervation along the dendritic tree showed no significant difference between CCKBCs and PVBCs.
source: We found that CCKBCs and PVBCs innervated their postsynaptic partners with similar number of boutons (Figure 4G), moreover, the average distance of the innervation along the dendritic tree (Figure 4H), the number of the contacts established on the perisomatic region (Figure 4I) and the ratio of perisomatic contacts among all boutons showed no significant difference (Figure 4J, all M-W test, p>0.05).

claim: The number of contacts established on the perisomatic region showed no significant difference between CCKBCs and PVBCs.

claim: The ratio of perisomatic contacts among all boutons showed no significant difference between CCKBCs and PVBCs.

claim: 7.89% of CCKBCs restricted their innervation exclusively to the perisomatic region (ratio of perisomatic contacts = 1).
source: Interestingly, there was only a small population of BCs, which restricted their innervation exclusively to the perisomatic region (i.e. ratio of perisomatic contacts = 1, 7.89% of CCKBCs and 3.84% of PVBCs, n = 3 and 1, respectively, Figure 4J), but most of the cells also contacted the dendrites with several synapses (92.11% of CCKBCs and 96.16% of PVBCs, n = 35 and 25, respectively).

claim: 3.84% of PVBCs restricted their innervation exclusively to the perisomatic region (ratio of perisomatic contacts = 1).

claim: The amplitude of the first IPSC is correlated with the number of the perisomatic boutons.
source: By analyzing the potential relationship between the electrophysiological properties of inhibitory connections and their underlying structural features, we found that the amplitude of the first IPSC is correlated with the number of the perisomatic boutons, but not with the total number of contacts (n = 20 CCKBC and 19 PVBC pairs, Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A-B

claim: The amplitude of the first IPSC is not correlated with the total number of contacts.
source: By analyzing the potential relationship between the electrophysiological properties of inhibitory connections and their underlying structural features, we found that the amplitude of the first IPSC is correlated with the number of the perisomatic boutons, but not with the total number of contacts (n = 20 CCKBC and 19 PVBC pairs, Figure 5A–B).

claim: The charge transfer of three IPSCs showed higher correlation with the number of perisomatic contacts than with the total number of contacts.
source: The charge transfer of three IPSCs also showed higher correlation with the number of perisomatic contacts than with the total number of contacts (Figure 5C and D).

claim: The inhibitory efficacy of both BCs may depend more on the number of perisomatic synapses than the total number of synapses.
source: Moreover, the inhibitory efficacy of both BCs may depend more on the number of perisomatic synapses than the total number of synapses as suggested by Figure 5E–H.
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 5E-H

claim: The area affected by gabazine puffs has a radius of ~50 µm, which can largely cover the perisomatic region of PNs.
source: By defining the furthest location along the dendrites where somatic gabazine puffs still had a significant effect on the GABA-evoked IPSC amplitude (M-W test p<0.05), we estimated that the area affected by gabazine puffs has a radius of ~50 µm, which can largely cover the perisomatic region of PNs (Figure 6C) (Vereczki et al., 2016).
evidence: Experimental determination shown in Figure 6C with citation to previous work

claim: Both the IPSC charge and the inhibitory efficacy were significantly reduced when the perisomatic contacts were blocked.
source: We found that both the IPSC charge and the inhibitory efficacy were significantly reduced when the perisomatic contacts were blocked (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: Pharmacological manipulation experiments shown in Figure 6G,H

claim: In pairs without perisomatic inhibitory inputs, a significantly weaker inhibitory effect could still be measured.
source: It should be noted, however, that in pairs without perisomatic inhibitory inputs (either by lacking a priori or by functional elimination with gabazine application) we could still measure - albeit a significantly weaker - inhibitory effect (Figure 6J), implying that although perisomatic inputs are the major determinant in controlling PN spiking, yet a summation of sufficient numbers of dendritic inputs can also influence the output of the postsynaptic cell.
evidence: Data from gabazine experiments shown in Figure 6J with inference about dendritic input contribution

claim: Perisomatic inputs are the major determinant in controlling PN spiking.
source: It should be noted, however, that in pairs without perisomatic inhibitory inputs (either by lacking a priori or by functional elimination with gabazine application) we could still measure - albeit a significantly weaker - inhibitory effect (Figure 6J), implying that although perisomatic inputs are the major determinant in controlling PN spiking, yet a summation of sufficient numbers of dendritic inputs can also influence the output of the postsynaptic cell.
evidence: Inference from pharmacological manipulation experiments shown in Figure 6J

claim: A summation of sufficient numbers of dendritic inputs can also influence the output of the postsynaptic cell.

claim: The number of perisomatic contacts from individual BCs was very variable on the Kv2.1-labeled profiles (ranging from 1 to 12 per Kv2.1-labeled cell, CV = 0.54 ± 0.03).
source: We found that the number of perisomatic contacts from individual BCs was very variable on the Kv2.1-labeled profiles (ranging from 1 to 12 per Kv2.1-labeled cell, CV = 0.54 ± 0.03, Figure 8C), and showed no correlation with the number of perisomatic contacts on the intracellularly-labeled postsynaptic PN (Figure 8D).
evidence: Analysis of Kv2.1 immunostaining data shown in Figure 8C

claim: The number of perisomatic contacts from individual BCs showed no correlation with the number of perisomatic contacts on the intracellularly-labeled postsynaptic PN.

claim: The ratio of the contacts targeting the perisomatic region was variable for CCKBCs (48.6 ± 3.1%, range: 16.5–81.1%).
source: The ratio of the contacts targeting the perisomatic region (i.e. on Kv2.1-labeled soma and proximal dendrites) was variable (CCKBCs: 48.6 ± 3.1%, range: 16.5–81.1%; PVBCs: 51.6 ± 3.5%, range: 17.4–84.9%) and formed a continuous distribution for both BC types (Figure 8E).
evidence: Analysis of Kv2.1 immunostaining data shown in Figure 8E

claim: The ratio of the contacts targeting the perisomatic region was variable for PVBCs (51.6 ± 3.5%, range: 17.4–84.9%).
source: The ratio of the contacts targeting the perisomatic region (i.e. on Kv2.1-labeled soma and proximal dendrites) was variable (CCKBCs: 48.6 ± 3.1%, range: 16.5–81.1%; PVBCs: 51.6 ± 3.5%, range: 17.4–84.9%) and formed a continuous distribution for both BC types (Figure 8E).

claim: The ratio of perisomatic contacts formed a continuous distribution for both BC types.

claim: There was no correlation between the ratio of perisomatic contacts obtained at the population level and those observed in the paired recordings.
source: We found no correlation between the ratio of perisomatic contacts obtained at the population level and those observed in the paired recordings (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A

claim: BCs with high ratio of perisomatic contacts at the population level tend to form more contacts on the perisomatic region of individual target cells.
source: However, the relationship between the average number of perisomatic contacts on Kv2.1-labeled profiles and the average ratio of perisomatic contacts at the population level (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D) implied that those cells that tend to target the perisomatic region at higher ratio at the population level, they also form more contacts on this membrane region of individual target cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B-D

claim: BCs with high ratio of perisomatic contacts can control the spiking activity of the postsynaptic cells more effectively.
source: This feature enables the BCs with high ratio of perisomatic contacts to control the spiking activity of the postsynaptic cells more effectively.
evidence: Inference from the relationship between perisomatic contact ratio and inhibitory efficacy

claim: Both CCKBCs and PVBCs tend to target the perisomatic region of PNs as a population.
source: These data together indicate that both CCKBCs and PVBCs tend to target the perisomatic region of PNs as a population, however, there is a marked variability in the number and ratio of the perisomatic contacts of individual BCs targeting different PNs, implying a variable inhibitory effect on distinct postsynaptic partners.

claim: There is a marked variability in the number and ratio of the perisomatic contacts of individual BCs targeting different PNs.

claim: The impact of the inhibitory control provided by single BCs onto distinct postsynaptic partners can significantly vary.
source: (4) The innervation pattern of individual BCs shows a high variability, therefore the impact of the inhibitory control provided by single BCs onto distinct postsynaptic partners can also significantly vary.
evidence: Inference from variability in innervation patterns

claim: The efficacy of control CCKBCs and PVBCs exhibit on PN firing is surprisingly similar.
source: Analogous to what was found in the hippocampus (Szabó et al., 2010; Hefft and Jonas, 2005; Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006), some characteristics of the output synapses of CCKBCs and PVBCs are slightly different, yet the efficacy of control these GABAergic cells exhibit on PN firing is surprisingly similar.
evidence: Comparison with hippocampal findings cited from previous studies

claim: Both cell types gave rise to synaptic currents with fast rise time, indicating the perisomatic origin of the postsynaptic events recorded in the PNs.
source: Both cell types gave rise to synaptic currents with fast rise time, indicating the perisomatic origin of the postsynaptic events recorded in the PNs.
evidence: Inference from IPSC kinetics measurements

claim: The difference in rise times between CCKBCs and PVBCs might derive from the spatiotemporal profile of neurotransmitter release.
source: This data indicates that the difference in rise times might derive from the spatiotemporal profile of neurotransmitter release, as it was described in the hippocampus (Bucurenciu et al., 2008; Lenkey et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference with citation to hippocampal studies

claim: The distinct release machinery might be responsible for the observed differences in the latency of the responses.
source: The distinct release machinery might also be responsible for the observed differences in the latency of the responses.
evidence: Speculation about mechanism underlying latency differences

claim: The innervation pattern of BCs in the BA resembles the properties of neocortical basket cells.
source: This innervation pattern resembles the properties of neocortical basket cells, as they also innervate distal dendritic regions of PNs with several synapses (Tamás et al., 2000; Kubota et al., 2015; Kisvárday et al., 2002).
evidence: Comparison with neocortical findings cited from previous studies

claim: BCs in the BA might be able to influence local dendritic computations by innervating distal dendritic segments.
source: The functional implication of the presence of both somatic and dendritic inhibitory inputs from the same cell requires more investigations, however, BCs in the BA -besides controlling action potential generation and somatic signal integration (present study)- might be able to influence local dendritic computations by innervating distal dendritic segments (Müllner et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculation about functional implications with citation

claim: In the neocortical and amygdalar microcircuits, BCs might have a dual function, as their output synapses are in the position to control both the input and output features of PNs.
source: Our results thus may suggest that in the neocortical and amygdalar microcircuits, in sharp contrast to that observed in the hippocampus (Miles et al., 1996), BCs might have a dual function, as their output synapses are in the position to control both the input and output features of PNs.
evidence: Inference from innervation pattern data with comparison to hippocampus

claim: The presence of multiple release sites at the axon terminals of CCKBCs in the BA is typical.
source: Although a tendency could be observed that PVBCs might establish more contacts than CCKBCs, the inhibitory efficacy of these two cell populations was similar, which can be, at least partially, explained by the fact that the presence of multiple release sites at the axon terminals of CCKBCs in the BA (as in other cortical regions) is typical (Katona et al., 2001; Yoshida et al., 2011).
evidence: Explanation with citations to previous studies

claim: Categorization of interneurons into perisomatic and dendrite-targeting cells expressing PV and CCK like in the hippocampus is not possible in the BA.
source: Between these two extremes, the innervation patterns of BCs formed a continuum, therefore categorization of these interneurons into perisomatic and dendrite-targeting cells expressing PV and CCK like in the hippocampus (Cope et al., 2002; Buhl et al., 1994; Szabó et al., 2014) is not possible in the BA.
evidence: Inference from innervation pattern analysis with comparison to hippocampus

claim: The BA plays a crucial role in fear learning.
source: We have addressed these questions in the basal (basolateral) nucleus of the amygdala (BA), a cortical structure that plays a crucial role in fear learning (Armony et al., 1995; Herry et al., 2008; Pape and Pare, 2010).
evidence: Statement about BA function with citations to previous studies

claim: Fear learning can be bidirectionally regulated by optogenetic manipulation of the activity of PV-containing interneurons in the BA.
source: As fear learning can be bidirectionally regulated by optogenetic manipulation of the activity of PV-containing interneurons in the BA (Wolff et al., 2014), our data suggests that the effect of manipulation of CCKBC functions at the behavioral level might be comparable to that observed in the case of PV-expressing interneurons on the BA network output.
evidence: Citation to previous optogenetic study with inference about CCKBCs

claim: The effect of manipulation of CCKBC functions at the behavioral level might be comparable to that observed in the case of PV-expressing interneurons on the BA network output.
source: As fear learning can be bidirectionally regulated by optogenetic manipulation of the activity of PV-containing interneurons in the BA (Wolff et al., 2014), our data suggests that the effect of manipulation of CCKBC functions at the behavioral level might be comparable to that observed in the case of PV-expressing interneurons on the BA network output.
evidence: Inference from similarity in inhibitory efficacy between CCKBCs and PVBCs

claim: AACs and PVBCs are heavily innervated by local PNs.
source: Morphological data (Smith et al., 2000) and unpublished observations from our lab showed that AACs and PVBCs are heavily innervated by local PNs, whereas CCKBCs lack the strong local feedback excitation.
evidence: Citation to previous morphological study and unpublished observations

claim: CCKBCs lack the strong local feedback excitation.
source: Morphological data (Smith et al., 2000) and unpublished observations from our lab showed that AACs and PVBCs are heavily innervated by local PNs, whereas CCKBCs lack the strong local feedback excitation.
evidence: Citation to previous morphological study and unpublished observations

claim: AACs and PVBCs might be involved in local feedback inhibitory circuits, and shape the firing of PNs even at low or moderate network activity levels.
source: These results imply that AACs and PVBCs might be involved in local feedback inhibitory circuits, and shape the firing of PNs even at low or moderate network activity levels.
evidence: Inference from connectivity patterns

claim: Local PNs may recruit CCKBCs to provide feedback inhibition only when the BA network activity is elevated, or together with a concomitant activation of extra-amygdalar, e.g. subcortical afferents.
source: On the other hand, local PNs may recruit CCKBCs to provide feedback inhibition only when the BA network activity is elevated, or together with a concomitant activation of extra-amygdalar, e.g. subcortical afferents.
evidence: Speculation about CCKBC recruitment based on connectivity patterns

claim: Perisomatic region of cortical principal neurons is a critical site for the input integration and for the generation of the action potential.
source: Perisomatic region of cortical principal neurons (PNs), comprising the cell body, proximal dendrites and the axon initial segment, is a subcellular domain that is a critical site for the input integration and for the generation of the action potential, the output of neurons.
evidence: Statement of established neuroscience knowledge

claim: Inhibitory inputs arriving onto the perisomatic region are in a position to powerfully regulate the firing of individual PNs and to synchronize the activity of large neuronal ensembles.
source: Inhibitory inputs arriving onto this region are in a position to powerfully regulate the firing of individual PNs and to synchronize the activity of large neuronal ensembles, leading to an efficient control of neural processing within local networks (Buhl et al., 1994; Cobb et al., 1995; Miles et al., 1996).
evidence: Statement with citations to previous studies

claim: Two major types of GABAergic cells are known to innervate the perisomatic region in all cortical areas: axo-axonic cells and basket cells.
source: Two major types of GABAergic cells are known to innervate the perisomatic region in all cortical areas: axo-axonic cells form synapses exclusively on the axon initial segment of PNs, while basket cells (BCs) target the soma and proximal dendrites (Somogyi et al., 1983; Somogyi, 1977; Veres et al., 2014; Gulyás et al., 1993).
evidence: Statement with citations to previous studies

claim: Axo-axonic cells form synapses exclusively on the axon initial segment of PNs.
source: Two major types of GABAergic cells are known to innervate the perisomatic region in all cortical areas: axo-axonic cells form synapses exclusively on the axon initial segment of PNs, while basket cells (BCs) target the soma and proximal dendrites (Somogyi et al., 1983; Somogyi, 1977; Veres et al., 2014; Gulyás et al., 1993).
evidence: Statement with citations to previous studies

claim: Basket cells target the soma and proximal dendrites.
source: Two major types of GABAergic cells are known to innervate the perisomatic region in all cortical areas: axo-axonic cells form synapses exclusively on the axon initial segment of PNs, while basket cells (BCs) target the soma and proximal dendrites (Somogyi et al., 1983; Somogyi, 1977; Veres et al., 2014; Gulyás et al., 1993).
evidence: Statement with citations to previous studies

claim: Basket cells are usually divided into two groups by the mutually exclusive expression of neurochemical markers: parvalbumin (PV) and cholecystokinin (CCK).
source: The latter interneuron type is usually divided into two groups by the mutually exclusive expression of neurochemical markers: the calcium binding protein parvalbumin (PV) and the neuropeptide cholecystokinin (CCK).
evidence: Statement of established classification in neuroscience

claim: The two types of basket cells have been proposed to contribute differently to network operations.
source: By having distinct functional characteristics, the two types of basket cells have been proposed to contribute differently to network operations (Armstrong and Soltesz, 2012; Bartos and Elgueta, 2012; Freund and Katona, 2007).
evidence: Statement with citations to previous reviews

claim: Parvalbumin-containing basket cells play a primary role in controlling and synchronizing the firing of PNs in large ensembles during distinct brain states.
source: Parvalbumin-containing basket cells (PVBCs) play a primary role in controlling and synchronizing the firing of PNs in large ensembles during distinct brain states (Sohal et al., 2009; Stark et al., 2014; Schlingloff et al., 2014; Gulyás et al., 2010; Tukker et al., 2013) as well as in gain control of sensory processes (Atallah et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement with citations to previous studies

claim: Parvalbumin-containing basket cells play a role in gain control of sensory processes.
source: Parvalbumin-containing basket cells (PVBCs) play a primary role in controlling and synchronizing the firing of PNs in large ensembles during distinct brain states (Sohal et al., 2009; Stark et al., 2014; Schlingloff et al., 2014; Gulyás et al., 2010; Tukker et al., 2013) as well as in gain control of sensory processes (Atallah et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement with citations to previous studies

claim: Much less is known about the function of cholecystokinin-expressing basket cells due to the lack of selective genetic tools.
source: In contrast, due to the lack of selective genetic tools, much less is known about the function of cholecystokinin-expressing basket cells (CCKBCs).
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: CCKBCs may provide a modulatory effect on network dynamics conveying information from subcortical areas about emotional, motivational and general physiological states.
source: In an influential review it has been proposed that these GABAergic cells may provide a modulatory effect on network dynamics conveying information from subcortical areas about emotional, motivational and general physiological states (Freund and Katona, 2007), a hypothesis that has not been challenged yet.
evidence: Citation to previous hypothesis

claim: In the hippocampus, both PVBCs and CCKBCs preferentially innervate the soma and proximal dendrites of pyramidal cells.
source: In the hippocampus, both PVBCs and CCKBCs preferentially innervate the soma and proximal dendrites of pyramidal cells (Halasy et al., 1996; Gulyás et al., 1993; Földy et al., 2010; Szabó et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement with citations to previous studies

claim: In the hippocampus, dendritic shafts of pyramidal cells are targeted by different interneurons expressing PV or CCK, whose axonal arbor largely avoids the pyramidal cell layer.
source: Their dendritic shafts, however, are targeted by different interneurons expressing PV or CCK, whose axonal arbor largely avoids the pyramidal cell layer (Buhl et al., 1994; Halasy et al., 1996; Cope et al., 2002; Szabó et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement with citations to previous studies

claim: The structural segregation of axon clouds of PV- and CCK-expressing GABAergic cells in the hippocampus secures the division of labor between perisomatic and dendrite-targeting interneurons.
source: The structural segregation of axon clouds of PV- and CCK-expressing GABAergic cells targeting distinct functional (perisomatic vs. dendritic) domains of pyramidal cells secures the division of labor between perisomatic and dendrite-targeting interneurons in the hippocampus.
evidence: Inference from structural organization with citations

claim: In the hippocampus, perisomatic inhibitory interneurons effectively control the output, the spiking of pyramidal cells.
source: Perisomatic inhibitory interneurons effectively control the output, the spiking of pyramidal cells, while the dendritic interneurons regulate their input properties (Miles et al., 1996; Pouille et al., 2013; Müllner et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement with citations to previous studies

claim: In the hippocampus, dendritic interneurons regulate the input properties of pyramidal cells.
source: Perisomatic inhibitory interneurons effectively control the output, the spiking of pyramidal cells, while the dendritic interneurons regulate their input properties (Miles et al., 1996; Pouille et al., 2013; Müllner et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement with citations to previous studies

claim: The clear structural arrangement in axonal projections of interneurons observed in the hippocampus is lacking in other cortical regions.
source: This clear structural arrangement in axonal projections of interneurons is lacking in other cortical regions, and single BCs can innervate both the perisomatic region of PNs as well as their more distal dendrites (Jiang et al., 2015; Kubota et al., 2015; Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1998).
evidence: Statement with citations to previous studies

claim: In other cortical regions, single BCs can innervate both the perisomatic region of PNs as well as their more distal dendrites.
source: This clear structural arrangement in axonal projections of interneurons is lacking in other cortical regions, and single BCs can innervate both the perisomatic region of PNs as well as their more distal dendrites (Jiang et al., 2015; Kubota et al., 2015; Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1998).
evidence: Statement with citations to previous studies

claim: PVBCs in neocortical areas innervate both the perisomatic region and more distal dendrites.
source: This latter finding, however, has been demonstrated so far only for PVBCs (Kubota et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to previous study

claim: Similar types of interneurons can be found in the BA as in other cortical regions, including the two types of BCs as well as axo-axonic cells.
source: Previous studies established that similar types of interneurons can be found in this region as in other cortical regions, including the two types of BCs as well as axo-axonic cells (Katona et al., 2001; McDonald and Betette, 2001; Sah et al., 2003; Spampanato et al., 2011; Bienvenu et al., 2012; Vereczki et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement with citations to previous studies

claim: The two BC types could inhibit PNs with the same efficacy and innervated the same somato-dendritic membrane surface of their postsynaptic partners.
source: Using in vitro paired recordings, pharmacological manipulations and correlated light and electron microscopy we found that the two BC types could inhibit PNs with the same efficacy and innervated the same somato-dendritic membrane surface of their postsynaptic partners.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Both BC types formed many synaptic contacts on distal dendrites at various ratios.
source: Besides innervating the perisomatic region, both BC types also formed many synaptic contacts on distal dendrites at various ratios, however, the main determinant of the efficacy of their spike inhibition was the number of the synaptic contacts targeting the perisomatic region.
evidence: Summary of morphological findings

claim: The main determinant of the efficacy of BC spike inhibition was the number of the synaptic contacts targeting the perisomatic region.
source: Besides innervating the perisomatic region, both BC types also formed many synaptic contacts on distal dendrites at various ratios, however, the main determinant of the efficacy of their spike inhibition was the number of the synaptic contacts targeting the perisomatic region.
evidence: Summary of correlation and pharmacological findings

claim: Both basket cell types can powerfully regulate the activity in amygdala networks predominantly via their perisomatic synapses.
source: Our results show that both basket cell types can powerfully regulate the activity in amygdala networks predominantly via their perisomatic synapses.
evidence: Summary conclusion from all experimental findings
